report.source_text: Serial MRI brain scans at presentation (A–C), 3 months (D–F) and 6 months (G–I) following initial presentation in a child with Baló’s concentric sclerosis. The initial MRI with contrast demonstrated a T2 hyperintense abnormality with central hypointense ring-like focus (A); alternating layers of high and low signal intensity giving it an ‘onion bulb’ appearance. There was central concentric contrast enhancement (B). At 3 months, the extent of the abnormality (D) and the area of contrast enhancement (E) had increased. At 6 months, the abnormality (G) and the contrast enhancement (H) had resolved. The abnormality showed central diffusion restriction with unrestricted diffusion in the periphery (C). The area of diffusion restriction increased in size at 3 months (F) and disappeared by 6 months (I).
report.temporal_cue: presentation and 3 months and 6 months later

clinician.final_diagnosis: Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion (Baló's concentric sclerosis)
clinician.trajectory_summary: An asymptomatic school-aged boy presented with incidental papilloedema (subsequently diagnosed as drusen) on routine optician examination. Non-enhanced head CT revealed a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity suggesting oedema. MRI brain demonstrated the pathognomonic 'onion bulb' appearance of Baló's concentric sclerosis with alternating circular layers of high and low signal intensity on T2-weighted images, central concentric contrast enhancement, and central diffusion restriction with unrestricted peripheral diffusion. At 3-month follow-up, MRI showed interval increase in lesion size, extent of T2 abnormality, contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction, prompting stereotactic brain biopsy to exclude tumor. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion. By 6 months, MRI demonstrated complete resolution of the abnormality, contrast enhancement, and diffusion restriction. The child remained asymptomatic throughout, received no treatment, and at 4-year follow-up showed continued lesion involution with no new brain or spinal lesions.
